blockMcqs.question: How do non-comparison sorts beat the O(n log n) wall?
options: They run on multiple cores in parallel
They use key values directly instead of comparing
They avoid recursion entirely
They keep the input nearly sorted
blockMcqs.explanation: The lower bound only binds sorts that decide via pairwise comparison.

blockMcqs.question: Why does merge sort need O(n) extra space?
options: It stores the full recursion tree in memory
Each recursive call copies the whole array
The merge step needs a buffer to combine halves
It builds a heap alongside the array
blockMcqs.explanation: Merging two sorted halves writes into a separate output buffer.

blockMcqs.question: When does quicksort degrade to O(n²)?
options: When the pivot is always the min or max
When the array has duplicate keys
When the array fits in cache
When recursion is replaced with a loop
blockMcqs.explanation: A min/max pivot leaves one side of size n−1, so depth grows to n.

blockMcqs.question: Why is heapsort usually slower than quicksort at equal big-O?
options: It needs O(n) extra memory
It makes more comparisons overall
Its index jumps thrash the CPU cache
It is not a comparison sort
blockMcqs.explanation: Sift-down hops between `2i+1`/`2i+2`, unlike quicksort's sequential scan.

blockMcqs.question: Why must any comparison sort make about n log n comparisons?
options: Each element must be compared to every other
Recursion depth is always log n
It must distinguish among n! possible orderings
Cache lines hold log n elements
blockMcqs.explanation: Each comparison gives one bit, so log₂(n!) ≈ n log n bits are needed.

blockMcqs.question: What is counting sort's main limitation?
options: It is unstable by nature
It needs O(k) space for the key range
It cannot run in linear time
It only works on sorted input
blockMcqs.explanation: A huge range like 64-bit keys would demand astronomically many buckets.

blockMcqs.question: How does quickselect reach O(n) average from quicksort's O(n log n)?
options: It uses a faster partition scheme
It recurses into only one side each step
It sorts both sides but stops early
It avoids comparisons using key values
blockMcqs.explanation: Discarding one half gives the geometric sum n + n/2 + … ≈ 2n.

blockMcqs.question: You need a stable sort with a guaranteed worst case. Pick:
options: Quicksort
Heapsort
Merge sort
Counting sort
blockMcqs.explanation: Quick isn't stable and risks O(n²); heap isn't stable; counting needs bounded keys.

blockMcqs.question: How does introsort avoid quicksort's O(n²) worst case?
options: It always uses the median as pivot
It switches to heapsort past a recursion-depth limit
It falls back to counting sort
It runs merge sort in parallel
blockMcqs.explanation: Deep recursion signals bad pivots, so it caps depth with a guaranteed O(n log n) sort.

blockMcqs.question: A query plan shows an "external merge / disk sort." What does it mean?
options: The sort spilled past work_mem onto disk
Two tables were joined incorrectly
The index was rebuilt during the query
Rows were already returned pre-sorted
blockMcqs.explanation: Exceeding the sort memory budget forces slow disk-backed runs.

blockMcqs.question: You only need the 3 largest of a million items. Best approach?
options: Full quicksort, then take the last three
Counting sort on the values
A size-k heap or quickselect
Merge sort for stability
blockMcqs.explanation: Both skip the full O(n log n) order, costing only O(n) or O(n log k).
